[EFFECT]
The day of the week influences demand in a non-monotonic, categorical way — there is no simple "higher day number means more or fewer bikes." Weekends (Saturday = 6 and Sunday = 0) show the widest swings: when other conditions align well (e.g. good weather, midday hours), they can push predicted demand the highest of any day, reaching SHAP contributions of about +0.6 in log space; but during off-peak hours on those same days, the contribution can drop to around −0.9, the most extreme negative of any day. Weekdays (Monday through Friday) produce a narrower, more moderate range of contributions roughly centred near zero, meaning the model treats them as close to the baseline demand level. Friday (5) shows a slightly wider positive spread than Monday through Wednesday, hinting at elevated end-of-week ridership.

[IMPORTANCE]
Weekday is the **4th most important feature** out of nine, with an importance score of 0.173. It sits well below hour of the day (0.833) but is comparable to year (0.200) and temperature (0.197), and clearly outweighs month, humidity, weather, wind speed, and holiday.

[RECOMMENDATION]
Because Saturdays and Sundays can produce both the biggest demand spikes and the sharpest off-peak troughs within the same day, staffing and bike redistribution plans for weekends should be more flexible and hour-sensitive than weekday plans — concentrate resources around peak leisure hours and scale back during early morning lows, rather than applying a flat weekend allocation.
